papers.title_in_file: Review of deep learning: concepts, CNN architectures, challenges, applications, future directions
papers.version_note: The file is the QUT eprints author-manuscript copy of the Journal of Big Data 2021, 8:53 survey. It has a one-page QUT cover sheet, so PDF page N is journal page N-1 (the journal's 'Page 2 of 74' is PDF p.3). The article text is the same paper the record names. The text layer holds the paper once.
sections_read: Challenges (limitations) of deep learning and alternate solutions

figures.shows: Search framework flow diagram with three stages (identification, screening, selection) and five colour-coded categories (introduction and definition, CNN architectures, challenges, applications, other). Printed counts: collected from databases 574, 972, 986, 2013, 128; other sources 10, 19, 12, 10, 0; duplicates removed (3891) 493, 703, 911, 1689, 95; screened on title and abstract (337) 68, 62, 90, 97, 20; excluded (3554) 425, 641, 821, 1592, 75; included (337) 68, 62, 90, 97, 20.

figures.shows: Journals cited in the review, with columns IF 2019, CiteScore 2019, publisher and homepage; for example Pattern Recognition 7.196/13.1 (Elsevier), Nature Medicine 36.130/45.9, Nature 42.779/51, Journal of Big Data (no IF)/6.1 (Springer), IEEE Access 3.745/3.9, Electronics 2.412/1.9 (MDPI).

figures.shows: Three nested circles: Artificial Intelligence (a program that can sense, reason, act and adapt) contains Machine Learning (algorithms whose performance improves as they are exposed to more data over time), which contains Deep Learning (subset of machine learning in which multilayered neural networks learn from vast amount of data).
figures.confirmed_by: DL, a subset of ML (Fig. 2), is inspired by the information processing patterns found in the human brain.

figures.shows: Two pipelines classifying cat/dog images. Machine learning: preprocessing, then features extraction, then features selection, then classification. Deep learning: a single deep learning model, then classification.
figures.confirmed_by: DL enables learning and classification to be achieved in a single shot (Fig. 3).

figures.shows: Horizontal bars of ImageNet top-5 error rate (x axis 0 to 30), labelled: SENet 2.25, ResNeXt 3.03, Inception v4 3.08, ResNet 3.5, Inception v3 3.57, Inception v2 4.8, Human 5 (red bar), GoogleNet 6.7, VGG 7.3, ZFNet 11.7, AlexNet 16.4, XRCE 25.8, NEC-UIUC 28.2. The models below the human bar are the later architectures.
figures.confirmed_by: Recently, DL performance has come to exceed human performance on tasks such as image classification (Fig. 4).

figures.shows: Example RvNN tree. Semantic representations of three regions feed neural networks that each output a score and a compositional vector, merged hierarchically into a root vector.
figures.confirmed_by: An example RvNN tree is shown in Fig. 5.

figures.shows: Unfolded RNN over four time steps: input layer (green) feeds a hidden layer (orange) with horizontal recurrent arrows, which feeds an output layer (blue).
figures.confirmed_by: For a given input sequence, a typical unfolded RNN diagram is illustrated in Fig. 6.

figures.shows: CNN for image classification: input image of a dog, convolution layer, ReLU layer, pooling layer, fully connected layer, output classes Dog / Not Dog.
figures.confirmed_by: An example of CNN architecture for image classification is illustrated in Fig. 7.

figures.shows: Five steps (Step-1 to Step-5) of a 2x2 kernel [0 1; -1 2] sliding with stride one over a 4x4 input [1 0 -2 1; -1 0 1 2; 0 2 1 0; 1 0 0 1], filling a 3x3 output feature map. The entries computed in steps 1 to 5 are 1, 0, 4, 4, 1.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 8 graphically illustrates the primary calculations executed at each step.

figures.shows: A 4x4 input grid [4 25 44 10; 8 14 8 33; 17 2 16 34; 5 13 24 7] with the 2x2 average pooling output [12 23; 9 20], the max pooling output [25 44; 17 34], and the global average pooling output 16.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 9 illustrates these three pooling operations.

figures.shows: Fully connected layer drawing. Input nodes feed hidden nodes, then a column of flattened feature values (0.1, 0.2, 0.9, 0.2, 0.9, 0.1, 0.2), then two output nodes Dog and Not Dog. The note says 'These connections are repeated for each node'.
figures.confirmed_by: The output of the FC layer represents the final CNN output, as illustrated in Fig. 10.

figures.shows: Three panels of red and green points with a fitted boundary: Underfitting (near-straight line), Overfitting (wiggly boundary following the points), Balanced (smooth boundary). No axes values.
figures.confirmed_by: These three types are illustrated in Fig. 11.

figures.shows: MLP structure: three data-sample nodes fully connected to three nodes with biases b1, b2, b3, with the weight W (superscript 2, subscript 11) marked on one connection.
figures.confirmed_by: So, Fig. 12 shows the weight on a connection from the

figures.shows: Two-layer network with three input nodes (B1), three hidden nodes (B1) and three output nodes (b2), labelled 'Hidden weight' and 'Output weight'. The caption reads 'Neuron activation functions', which does not match the drawing.
figures.confirmed_by: two layers in our neural network that is shown in Fig. 13

figures.shows: Brief overview of CNN architectures (continues on p.29), with columns model, main finding, depth, dataset, error rate, input size and year. Examples: AlexNet depth 8, ImageNet error 16.4, 227x227x3, 2012; VGG depth 16/19, error 7.3, 2014; GoogLeNet depth 22, error 6.7, 2015; ResNet depth 152, error 3.57, 2016; Inception-ResNet-v2 depth 164, error 3.52; DenseNet depth 201; MobileNet-v2 depth 53; CapsuleNet MNIST error 0.00855, 28x28x1, 2018; HRNetV2 ImageNet error 5.4, 2020.
figures.confirmed_by: Table 2 presents the brief overview of CNN architectures.

figures.shows: LeNet architecture: input 32x32; C1 28*28*6; S2 14*14*6 (subsampling); C3 10*10*16; S4 5*5*16; C5 120; F6 84; output 10, with full and Gaussian connections.
figures.confirmed_by: The history of deep CNNs began with the appearance of LeNet [89] (Fig. 14).

figures.shows: AlexNet architecture: 227x227x3 input; conv 11x11 stride 4, 96 kernels (55x55); overlapping max pool 3x3 stride 2 (27); conv 5x5 pad 2, 256 kernels; pool (13); three conv 3x3 layers (384, 384, 256 kernels); pool (6x6, 9216 values); FC 4096; FC 4096; 1000-way softmax.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 15 illustrates the basic design of the AlexNet architecture.

figures.shows: Network-in-network: stacked blocks, each with a convolution followed by small multilayer perceptron layers, ending in a final low-dimensional output.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 16 shows the structure of the network.

figures.shows: ZefNet architecture: 224 image, filter size 7 stride 2, 3x3 max pooling stride 2, five layers with feature-map sizes 110, 26, 13, 13, 13 and 96/256/384 channels, two 4096-unit layers and a softmax output.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 17 shows the structure of the network.

figures.shows: VGG: input, repeated blocks of Conv.+ReLU layers followed by max pooling, then three FC layers and softmax.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 18 shows the structure of the network.

figures.shows: Inception block: input from previous layer feeds four branches (1x1 conv then 3x3 conv; 1x1 conv then 5x5 conv; 3x3 max pooling then 1x1 conv; 1x1 conv), joined by a concatenation.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 19 illustrates the inception block architecture.

figures.shows: ResNet block: input goes through Weight layer (1), ReLU, further layers, Weight layer (m), is added to the input via a skip connection, then ReLU.
figures.confirmed_by: This is illustrated in Fig. 20, which contains the fundamental ResNet block diagram.

figures.shows: Inception residual unit: ReLU activation, two branches of 1x1 conv, 3x3 conv (and 5x5 conv in one branch), a 1x1 conv, summed with the skip connection, then ReLU activation.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 21 shows The basic block diagram for Inception Residual unit.

figures.shows: DenseNet: layers H1 to H4 (BN-ReLU-Conv) producing x1 to x4, with coloured arcs from every earlier feature map to every later layer, and a transition layer.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 22 shows the architecture of DenseNet Network.

figures.shows: ResNeXt block: 256-dimensional input split into 32 paths, each 256,1x1,4 then 4,3x3,4 then 4,1x1,256, summed with a skip connection into a 256-dimensional output.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 23 shows the ResNext building blocks.

figures.shows: Xception block: input from previous layer, a 1x1 convolution, output channels split over seven 3x3 convolutions, then a 1x1 convolution.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 24 shows the Xception block architecture.

figures.shows: CapsNet: 9x9 input patch, ReLU Conv1 (256 channels, 20x20), PrimaryCaps (32 groups of 8D, 6x6), DigitalCaps (10 x 16); decoder of FC ReLU 512, FC ReLU 1024, FC Sigmoid 784, with a reconstruction target.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 25 represents the complete CapsNet encoding and decoding processes.

figures.shows: HRNet: four parallel resolution streams with conv blocks (x3), strided convs and upsampling that repeatedly exchange information across resolutions, with output heads on the right.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 26 illustrates the general architecture of HRNet.

figures.shows: Performance (y) against amount of data (x), no numeric ticks. The Deep learning curve starts low, keeps rising and ends higher. The Older learning algorithms curve rises quickly, plateaus and is overtaken by deep learning at moderate data amounts.
figures.confirmed_by: as the data increases, an extra well-behaved performance model can be achieved (Fig. 27)

figures.shows: Transfer learning: source data trains a source model with source labels (large amount of data/labels); learned knowledge is transferred to a target model with target data and target labels (small amount of data/labels).
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 28 illustrates the conceptual diagram of the TL technique.

figures.shows: Workflow of DL tasks: pre-processing (crop, resize), dataset partitioning, data IO, data sampling, data augmentation, model selection/model fitting, model inference, evaluation, result; a Model Zoo box is linked for model initialization and comparison.
figures.confirmed_by: there is fundamental overlap in the pipeline implementation of these applications as shown in Fig. 30.

papers.what_it_is: A broad survey (Journal of Big Data 2021) of deep learning concepts, CNN architectures from AlexNet to HRNet, challenges and remedies, medical imaging applications, CPU/GPU/FPGA computing, metrics and frameworks, built from more than 300 reviewed papers; it reports no experiments of its own.

assertions.value: The authors state that they reviewed research papers published during 2010–2020, mainly from 2020 and 2019 with some from 2021, and that they reviewed more than 300 papers on various DL topics.
quotes: published during 2010– 2020, mainly from the years of 2020 and 2019 with some papers from 2021
We have reviewed more than 300 papers on various DL topics.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own survey scope in the Survey methodology section.
assertions.reader_inference: No inclusion or exclusion criteria beyond publisher preference and keywords are given in the text; the Figure 1 counts (337 included) are the only screening record.

assertions.value: The authors report 108 papers from 2020, 76 papers from 2019 and 48 papers from 2018 among the papers reviewed.
quotes: There are 108 papers from the year 2020, 76 papers from the year 2019, and 48 papers from the year 2018.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own description of the survey corpus.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 1: the search framework reports about 337 articles included in the review after about 3891 duplicates were removed and about 3554 articles were excluded; the included articles split into about 68 (introduction and definition), about 62 (CNN architectures), about 90 (challenges), about 97 (applications) and about 20 (other).
quotes: Figure 1 shows our search structure of the survey paper.
Search framework
assertions.certainty_reason: Counts read from a flow diagram; the text does not restate them.
assertions.reader_inference: The 337 included articles are roughly consistent with 'more than 300 papers' in the text, but the reference list holds 343 entries.

assertions.value: The authors claim this is the first review that almost provides a deep survey of the most important aspects of deep learning.
quotes: This is the first review that almost provides a deep survey of the most important aspects of deep learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: Priority and novelty claim by the authors, without comparison against other reviews.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper cites other reviews that covered single topics but gives no systematic comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that DL has outperformed well-known ML techniques in many domains, including cybersecurity, natural language processing, bioinformatics, robotics and control, and medical information processing.
quotes: More importantly, DL has outperformed well-known ML techniques in many domains, e.g., cybersecurity, natural language processing, bioinformatics, robotics and control, and medical information processing, among many others.
assertions.certainty_reason: General claim in the abstract without a head-to-head comparison in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no table comparing DL to classical ML on matched tasks.

assertions.value: The authors describe DL as a subset of ML, inspired by the information processing patterns found in the human brain.
quotes: DL, a subset of ML (Fig. 2), is inspired by the information processing patterns found in the human brain.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of DL in the Background section.

assertions.value: The authors state that conventional ML classification requires several sequential steps (pre-processing, feature extraction, wise feature selection, learning, classification), whereas DL enables learning and classification in a single shot.
quotes: Achieving the classification task using conventional ML techniques requires several sequential steps, specifically pre-processing, feature extraction, wise feature selection, learning, and classification.
DL enables learning and classification to be achieved in a single shot (Fig. 3).
assertions.certainty_reason: Conceptual statement by the authors, supported only by a schematic.

assertions.value: The authors state that DL performance has come to exceed human performance on tasks such as image classification.
quotes: Recently, DL performance has come to exceed human performance on tasks such as image classification (Fig. 4).
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' summary statement, supported by a bar chart whose human baseline is not sourced in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The figure shows a human top-5 error of 5 percent; the text does not say where it comes from.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 4: ImageNet top-5 error bars give a human value of about 5; SENet about 2.25, ResNeXt about 3.03, Inception v4 about 3.08, ResNet about 3.5, Inception v3 about 3.57 and Inception v2 about 4.8 are below it; GoogleNet about 6.7, VGG about 7.3, ZFNet about 11.7, AlexNet about 16.4, XRCE about 25.8 and NEC-UIUC about 28.2 are above it.
quotes: Deep learning performance compared to human
Recently, DL performance has come to exceed human performance on tasks such as image classification (Fig. 4).
assertions.certainty_reason: Values taken from a chart whose sources are not given in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 2 lists ResNet at 3.57 and Inception-V4 at 3.08, whereas the figure lists ResNet at 3.5 and Inception v3 at 3.57, so the two sources differ slightly.

assertions.value: The authors report, citing a cited study, that a DL network had the same ability to diagnose disease as twenty-one board-certified dermatologists, using 129,450 images of 2032 diseases.
quotes: Esteva et al. [45] found that a DL network has the same ability to diagnose the disease as twenty-one board-certified dermatologists using 129,450 images of 2032 diseases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Result of another study reported by the survey.

assertions.value: The authors report that in grading prostate cancer US board-certified general pathologists achieved an average accuracy of 61%, while a cited Google AI achieved an average accuracy of 70%.
quotes: cancer, US board-certified general pathologists achieved an average accuracy of 61%, while the Google AI [44] outperformed these specialists by achieving an average accuracy of 70%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited single-study result.

assertions.value: The paper states that DL techniques are classified into three major categories: unsupervised, partially supervised (semi-supervised) and supervised.
quotes: DL techniques are classified into three major categories: unsupervised, partially supervised (semi-supervised) and supervised.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own taxonomy used to organise its sections.

assertions.value: The authors state that deep reinforcement learning was developed in 2013 with Google Deep Mind.
quotes: This technique was developed in 2013 with Google Deep Mind [55].
assertions.certainty_reason: Historical statement attributed to a cited work.
assertions.reader_inference: The cited reference is a 2015 Nature paper; the 2013 date is not explained in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that, compared with traditional supervised techniques, reinforcement learning is much more difficult because no straightforward loss function is available.
quotes: In comparison with traditional supervised techniques, performing this learning is much more difficult, as no straightforward loss function is available in the reinforcement learning technique.
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative statement without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that RNN sensitivity to exploding gradient and vanishing problems is one of the main issues with this approach.
quotes: sensitivity to the exploding gradient and vanishing problems represent one of the main issues with this approach
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement attributed to a cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that CNN is considered more powerful than RNN and that RNN includes less feature compatibility than CNN.
quotes: CNN is considered to be more powerful than RNN. RNN includes less feature compatibility when compared to CNN.
assertions.certainty_reason: Unsupported comparative claim; no evidence or citation given.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Feature compatibility' is not defined and no comparison is shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main benefit of CNN compared with its predecessors is that it automatically identifies the relevant features without any human supervision.
quotes: The main benefit of CNN compared to its predecessors is that it automatically identifies the relevant features without any human supervision [76].
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement attributed to a cited work.

assertions.value: The authors describe a commonly used CNN as similar to the multi-layer perceptron, with numerous convolution layers preceding sub-sampling (pooling) layers and FC layers at the end.
quotes: A commonly used type of CNN, which is similar to the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), consists of numerous convolution layers preceding sub-sampling (pooling) layers, while the ending layers are FC layers.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of the CNN structure it then analyses.

assertions.value: The authors state that each of the k feature maps h^k has a size of (m − n − 1), where the input is m × m × r and the kernels are n × n × q.
quotes: The input x of each layer in a CNN model is organized in three dimensions: height, width, and depth, or m × m × r
with a size of ( m − n − 1 ) each
assertions.certainty_reason: Formula as printed by the authors; it conflicts with their own later example.
assertions.reader_inference: The later CapsNet example computes 28 − 9 + 1 = 20, which implies m − n + 1 for stride 1 without padding, so the printed minus-one looks like a typo.

assertions.value: The authors state that weight sharing reduces the number of trainable network parameters and in turn helps the network enhance generalization and avoid overfitting.
quotes: The main reason to consider CNN is the weight sharing feature, which reduces the number of trainable network parameters and in turn helps the network to enhance generalization and to avoid overfitting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative benefit statement without measurement in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors illustrate the convolution operation with a 4 × 4 gray-scale image and a 2 × 2 random weight-initialized kernel, with no padding and a stride of one.
quotes: let us take an example of a 4 × 4 gray-scale image with a 2 × 2 random weight-initialized kernel.
However, padding to the input image is not applied in the previous example,
a stride of one (denoted for the selected step-size
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the settings of its own worked example.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 8: five convolution steps of a kernel over an input grid are drawn, and the output feature-map entries produced in the first five positions are about 1, about 0, about 4, about 4 and about 1.
quotes: The primary calculations executed at each step of convolutional layer
Figure 8 graphically illustrates the primary calculations executed at each step.
assertions.certainty_reason: Illustrative worked example read from a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: Step 1 checks by hand: the kernel [0 1; -1 2] over the top-left patch [1 0; -1 0] gives 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main shortfall of the pooling layer is that it can decrease overall CNN performance, because the layer helps determine whether a feature is present but focuses exclusively on its correct location, so the CNN model misses relevant information.
quotes: Sometimes, the overall CNN performance is decreased as a result; this represents the main shortfall of the pooling layer,
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative limitation of pooling stated without evidence.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence's wording is garbled: a pooling layer is generally described as keeping presence while discarding exact location, the reverse of what is printed.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 9: for the drawn 4 × 4 input grid, average pooling gives about 12, about 23, about 9 and about 20; max pooling gives about 25, about 44, about 17 and about 34; global average pooling gives about 16.
quotes: Figure 9 illustrates these three pooling operations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Worked illustration read from a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The averages (12.75, 23.75, 9.25, 20.25 and 16.5 for the global value) appear to have been truncated rather than rounded.

assertions.value: The authors state that ReLU is the most commonly used activation function in the CNN context.
quotes: ReLU: The mostly commonly used function in the CNN context.
assertions.certainty_reason: Usage statement without survey data.

assertions.value: The authors state that lower computational load is the main benefit of ReLU over the other activation functions.
quotes: Lower computational load is the main benefit of ReLU over the others.
assertions.certainty_reason: Unmeasured benefit claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that ReLU converts the whole values of the input to positive numbers.
quotes: It converts the whole values of the input to positive numbers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Descriptive statement that does not match the paper's own formula.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own formula is max(0, x), which maps negatives to zero, giving non-negative rather than positive outputs.

assertions.value: The authors state that Leaky ReLU ensures negative inputs are never ignored and is employed to solve the Dying ReLU problem.
quotes: Leaky ReLU: Instead of ReLU down-scaling the negative inputs, this activation function ensures these inputs are never ignored.
It is employed to solve the Dying ReLU problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: Description of a technique without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Leaky ReLU leak factor is commonly set to a very small value, such as 0.001.
quotes: It is commonly set to a very small value, such as 0.001.
assertions.certainty_reason: Usage statement without a source.

assertions.value: The authors state that dropout randomly drops neurons during each training epoch, which distributes feature selection power across the neurons and forces the model to learn different independent features.
quotes: During each training epoch, neurons are randomly dropped.
as well as forcing the model to learn different independent features.
assertions.certainty_reason: Description of a regularizer without experiments in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that batch normalization prevents the vanishing gradient problem from arising.
quotes: It prevents the problem of vanishing gradient from arising.
assertions.certainty_reason: Absolute claim without evidence.
assertions.reader_inference: Stated as complete prevention, which is stronger than a mitigation.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a small-sized dataset the CNN model converges faster and creates an extra-stable gradient using batch gradient descent.
quotes: For a small-sized dataset, the CNN model converges faster and creates an extra-stable gradient using BGD.
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative statement attributed to cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a large training dataset stochastic gradient descent is both more memory-effective and much faster than batch gradient descent, but takes extremely noisy steps that make convergence highly unstable.
quotes: For a large-sized training dataset, this technique is both more memory-effective and much faster than BGD.
which in turn causes the convergence behavior to become highly unstable.
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative statement attributed to cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that mini-batch gradient descent combines the advantages of batch and stochastic gradient descent, giving steady convergence, more computational efficiency and extra memory effectiveness.
quotes: Thus, it has a steady convergence, more computational efficiency and extra memory effectiveness.
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative statement without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the momentum factor value is maintained within the range 0 to 1, that a very low value loses the ability to avoid the local minimum, and that a high value converges more rapidly.
quotes: The momentum factor value is maintained within the range 0 to 1;
As the value of the momentum factor becomes very low, the model loses its ability to avoid the local bare minimum.
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative description of a hyperparameter effect without experiments.

assertions.value: The authors state that Adam is represented by the Hessian matrix, which employs a second-order derivative.
quotes: This is represented by the Hessian matrix, which employs a second-order derivative.
assertions.certainty_reason: Technical description by the authors that conflicts with their own next sentences.
assertions.reader_inference: The same section says Adam uses squared gradients to scale the learning rate and a moving average of the gradient, which are first-order quantities, so the Hessian statement looks mistaken.

assertions.value: The authors give an example that ten inputs fully connected to two neurons in the next layer give 20 connections (weights).
quotes: the number of connection between them is (10 ∗ 2 = 20 connection, weights)
assertions.certainty_reason: Arithmetic worked example in the paper's own text.

assertions.value: The authors state, based on their own experiments, that the most active solutions that may improve CNN performance are: expanding the dataset with data augmentation or transfer learning, increasing training time, increasing the depth (or width) of the model, adding regularization, and increasing hyperparameter tuning.
assertions.anchor: Improving performance of CNN, p.26; p.27
quotes: Based on our experiments in different DL applications [86–88].
Expand the dataset with data augmentation or use transfer learning
Increase the training time.
Increase the depth (or width) of the model.
Add regularization.
Increase hyperparameters tuning.
assertions.certainty_reason: Conclusion drawn from earlier work by the same authors; no data are shown here.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiments are in the authors' own cited papers, not reported in this review.

assertions.value: The authors state that the key upgrade in CNN performance occurred largely due to processing-unit reorganization and the development of novel blocks, and that the most novel developments in CNN architectures were performed on the use of network depth.
quotes: Conversely, it should be noted that the key upgrade in CNN performance occurred largely due to the processing-unit reorganization, as well as the development of novel blocks.
In particular, the most novel developments in CNN architectures were performed on the use of network depth.
assertions.certainty_reason: Interpretive synthesis by the authors without a quantitative attribution.

assertions.value: The authors state that two GPUs (NVIDIA GTX 580) were used in parallel to train AlexNet to overcome hardware limitations.
quotes: two GPUs (NVIDIA GTX 580) were used in parallel to train AlexNet
assertions.certainty_reason: Historical detail attributed to the AlexNet work.

assertions.value: The authors state that network-in-network employs global average pooling as a substitute for an FC layer, which enables a significant reduction in the number of model parameters.
quotes: As a substitution for a FC layer, the GAP is also employed, which represents the second novel concept and enables a significant reduction in the number of model parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to the cited NIN work; no numbers given.

assertions.value: The authors state that Zeiler and Fergus introduced DeconvNet (a multilayer de-convolutional neural network) in 2013, later known as ZefNet, to quantitatively visualize the network.
quotes: Zeiler and Fergus introduced DeconvNet (a multilayer de-convolutional neural network) in 2013 [97].
assertions.certainty_reason: Historical attribution to a cited paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 2 lists ZfNet under 2014 while this text says 2013.

assertions.value: The authors state that VGG's computational cost was excessive because it used around 140 million parameters, which was its main shortcoming.
quotes: computational cost was excessive due to its utilization of around 140 million parameters, which represented its main shortcoming
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited figure about VGG; the paper does not recompute it.

assertions.value: The authors state that VGG featured nineteen more layers than ZefNet and AlexNet.
quotes: it featured nineteen more layers than ZefNet [97] and AlexNet [30] to simulate the relations
